---
title: Representation learning
description: "Reuse learned customer or event context as features for separate prediction tasks."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose a retailer has trained the [customer-outcome model](customer-outcomes.qmd)
on purchase histories and seven-day inactivity labels. A different team wants
to predict spending over the next 30 days. It can test whether the first
model's learned customer context helps that new task before fitting another
history model end to end.

An embedding is a vector representation of an observation's context. This
use case keeps the exporting model fixed, produces vectors for customer
snapshots, and trains a separate predictor with the new task's labels.
The new predictor still needs training data and an independent evaluation.

## Reuse an already trained model

The customer example saves its trained schema and learned state as
`artifacts/customer-outcomes.rf`. Suppose your application has produced that
artifact and prepared snapshot requests with the same customer fields and
`recent_purchases` records, omitting `inactive_next_7_days`. Keep `customer_id`
and `cutoff` as source metadata.

This comparison keeps the original eligibility rule: each customer purchased
within the seven days before the snapshot cutoff. A spending task covering all
customers would need its own training population and evaluation of representation
coverage and quality.

Load that artifact and enable a root context export:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.load("artifacts/customer-outcomes.rf")
model.update(rf.where("address") == rf.Address(), embed=True)
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="customers/representation-requests.parquet",
    retain=("customer_id", "cutoff"),
)
result = model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

`embed=True` requests an export. It creates no new learning objective and does
not itself train the representation. Prediction uses the learned state from
the customer model.

The `sm` schema in that example uses two root summary outputs. Keep them in
`output_index` order when assembling features for one snapshot:

```python
snapshot_features = []
for row in result.to_pylist():
    root_outputs = sorted(
        (record for record in row["representations"] if record["path"] == []),
        key=lambda record: record["output_index"],
    )
    snapshot_features.append({
        "customer_id": row["inputs"]["customer_id"],
        "cutoff": row["inputs"]["cutoff"],
        "features": [value for record in root_outputs for value in record["embedding"]],
    })
```

The result is one feature vector per customer snapshot. A customer can have
many snapshots, so join the new spending label by both customer and cutoff.
Root context describes the whole observation. An event-level task instead
needs a representation at the matching event positions; see
[Reusable representations](../learn/reusable-representations.qmd) for branch
and leaf export choices, shapes, and a columnar extraction example.

## Train the separate task predictor

Prepare `spend_next_30_days` from the completed 30-day window after each
snapshot, with a fixed currency and refund policy. Fit a regressor on the
training snapshots' vectors and those labels. The exporting model stays fixed
while that regressor is trained.

Compare three inputs for the same predictor family and held-out snapshots:

| Input | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Existing customer features | How well does the current workflow perform? |
| Exported context vectors | What does the learned history representation contribute on its own? |
| Both together | Does the representation add useful information to existing features? |

Also compare with fitting the 30-day target directly in a history model when
that is affordable. MAE in source currency measures spending error; any
contact or offer policy needs its own decision metric.

Choose entity and time boundaries before training the exporting model or
the downstream predictor. A vector computed at a past cutoff must come from
an extractor whose training respects the evaluation boundary. Using future
records or held-out customer labels to train the extractor changes what the
downstream test measures.

## Choose the representation's learning signal

Supervised customer outcomes are one training signal. A reconstruction model
can instead learn by predicting selected values hidden inside historical
records. Its declared field types and nesting define the architecture; the
hidden values define the pretraining objectives.

Building a foundation model for your own structured data starts with this
broader pretraining and an intended reuse workflow. You can then adapt the
schema and fine-tune for labeled outcomes, or keep the pretrained model fixed
and export context for separate predictors. The
[pretraining tutorial](../learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) shows the
first route. Schema edits retain compatible learned state and initialize
incompatible parts according to the
[mutation rules](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd); reevaluate the adapted model.
For the reuse comparison on this page, keep the extractor fixed while fitting
the separate spending predictor.

A representation useful for inactivity need not provide useful product
similarity, segmentation, or anomaly scores. Define those tasks and test
their metrics explicitly. In particular, a candidate scorer does not
automatically produce user and item vectors whose dot product is a retrieval
score. [Recommendations](recommendations.qmd) separates that retrieval design
from candidate scoring.

The [representation-transfer evidence](../evidence/representation/reconstruction-transfer.html)
compares exported context with raw inputs, an untrained encoder, and a
corrupted-input control in its own synthetic task. Use that experiment to
understand the mechanism, then evaluate reuse on the customer outcome and
data population that matter to the application.
